I am a 50-year-old woman farmer in Quzhou. I have never been to school, but I have farmed this land since I was a young girl, and my mother and grandmother taught me everything I know. My family has about 8 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain.

This year, I will stick to what I know best: **winter wheat and summer maize** on all 8 mu. I thought about planting some cotton like my neighbor, but cotton needs spraying almost every week for bugs, and my back is not what it used to be. Wheat and maize feed my family and give us steady money. The wheat is already in the ground—I sowed it last October after the autumn harvest, just like everyone else in the village. Now it is greening up, and I need to topdress it with urea and irrigate it three times before harvest in early June. As soon as the wheat comes off, I will plant maize directly into the stubble without ploughing—that is how we have done it for years here, and it saves time and fuel before the summer rains.

For wheat, I use the improved variety Luyuan 502 that the government extension office gave out last year. It yields well and resists lodging. For maize, I will buy Denghai 605 hybrid seeds from the shop in town. My husband's cousin planted it last year and got over 1,100 jin per mu, so I trust it. I apply compound fertilizer as basal and topdress with urea when the wheat starts jointing. For maize, I put down compound fertilizer at sowing and side-dress with urea when the plants are knee-high. I spray pesticides about four times for each crop—mostly for aphids on wheat and corn borer on maize. I use rotary tillage before wheat sowing, but for maize I do no-tillage because the wheat stubble holds moisture and we are always racing the calendar between harvest and planting.
